inaugurate

/in-AW-gyuh-rayt/ - the stress falls on AW · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Inaugurate means to begin something — or install someone in office — with a formal ceremony that marks the start.

The city inaugurated its first light-rail line at dawn, with speeches, a brass band, and a ceremonial first ticket.

Example

The university inaugurated its new chancellor in the stone chapel — robes, the mace carried in, the 1854 charter read aloud — before she signed the register that every chancellor before her had signed.

Inaugurate is never a plain start: it is a beginning dressed in ceremony, whether a person is being installed in office or a building, service, or era is being formally opened. And watch the prefix — this in- is not the unit's 'not.' It is Latin in-, 'in, on': in Rome nothing official began until an augur read the omens in the flight of birds, and inaugurare meant to install someone once the signs approved.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

launch: To launch is to send something energetically on its way — a ship, a product, a campaign — with publicity but no required ritual. Inaugurate insists on the ceremony itself: the oath, the ribbon, the charter read aloud.

commence: To commence is simply to begin — the neutral, formal word for events and proceedings, asking nothing of the occasion. Inaugurate wraps the same beginning in ritual and marks it as historic.

induct: To induct is to admit a person into membership — a society, a hall of fame, an order of peers. Inaugurate installs a person in an office or opens something new to the world; you are inducted among equals, inaugurated into a presidency.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

conclude: to bring something formally to a close

decommission: to retire something officially from service

Where it sits · how much ceremony the beginning carries

open → inaugurate → enthrone

open vs. inaugurate: To open something is the plain, everyday start — weaker than inaugurate, which dresses the same beginning in ritual: an oath, a ribbon, a charter read aloud.

enthrone vs. inaugurate: Enthrone goes further than inaugurate: an inaugurated leader takes an oath and an office, while an enthroned one is crowned amid full royal pageantry.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: in, on (Latin) — not this unit's negating in-

Root — augur: the Roman omen-reader, who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds (Latin augur)

Suffix — -ate: verb

Put it together: A disguise to open the unit: the in- of inaugurate means 'in, on,' and nothing is negated. In Rome no consul took office and no temple opened until an augur — the official omen-reader — declared the bird-signs favorable; inaugurare meant to install with the omens' blessing. Every modern inauguration, oath or ribbon or fanfare, still carries that ceremonial DNA: a beginning is being made official.

Use the root in a new word: augur: The sold-out preview augured well for the play's long run, whatever the skeptics had predicted.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / ceremonial

Inaugurate is the ceremonial word for a beginning — presidents, chancellors, buildings, eras. If no ritual is in sight, plain open, begin, or launch is more honest; commence is the neutral formal 'begin'; induct admits a person to membership rather than office. The family travels with it: an inaugural address, given at the inauguration.
